_version_note: This catalog versions INDEPENDENTLY of the bundle that ships it. `generated` is when
entries were first extracted from the source page; `audited` is the last time they
were checked back against it. Density bands are comparable only within one `version`.
Why, and what depends on it: see the bundle README, 'Two clocks'.
_about: The shared pattern catalog. Inherited by every profile; never duplicated per
profile, because two copies of a catalog drift within about two edits.
A profile may `disable` entries, `adjust` their severity, or add entries of
its own — see profiles/technical/ for the pattern.
SEVERITY is how much weight one hit carries: 3 strong, 2 moderate, 1 weak
alone. CONFIDENCE is how much the source material and our own testing trust
the pattern: `high` means it rarely fires on good human writing, `medium`
means it fires sometimes, `contested` means it fires on legitimate prose
often enough that it should never be actioned without reading the hit.
Severity and confidence are separate axes on purpose. An intensifier tic is
low severity and contested; vague attribution is moderate severity and high
confidence. Collapsing them into one number is how a scanner starts telling
people their own writing is fake.
AUTHORING GOTCHA: `kind: lexical` patterns are wrapped in \b(?:...)\b
automatically, so an alternation ending in a bare prefix will not match its
own inflections — `navigate the complex` never matches `complexities`,
because \b finds no boundary mid-word. Spell out whole-word alternatives,
or use `kind: structural`, which is passed through with no wrapping.
TIER is the axis that matters most, and it is coarser than severity.
Tier A entries are ARTIFACTS — leaked citation markup, chatbot register,
unreplaced placeholders. They are near-zero false positive and dispositive
on a single occurrence, so they carry `always_flag` and bypass density
gating entirely. Everything else is STYLE, is meaningful only in aggregate,
and is density-gated. If you add an entry, be honest about which it is;
style dressed up as an artifact is how a scanner starts making accusations.
CALIBRATION TARGET: the source reports that an expert LLM user tagging ten
pages as AI-generated has probably made one false positive. About 10% is
the realistic ceiling for human experts. Any tool claiming better precision
than that on style alone is overclaiming, this one included.
ERA matters. The source list tracks vocabulary by generation, and the
generations turn over fast: the 2023-24 cohort (delve, tapestry, testament)
is largely trained out, while the mid-2025-onward cohort is participial —
emphasizing, highlighting, showcasing, enhance. An entry's `era` field
records which cohort it belongs to. Patterns expire; re-check the sources.
NO SINGLE PATTERN INDICATES AI AUTHORSHIP. These fire together or they are
noise. The source page is blunt about this and so is this catalog:
'Humans are notoriously bad at distinguishing human and LLM-generated
text.' It cites a 2025 preprint finding that even heavy LLM users judge
correctly about 90% of the time — one wrong call in ten. It also notes that
non-native English speakers are taught to avoid repeating words, which
produces the same surface features this catalog looks for.
So: signals for an author to weigh about their own draft. Never a verdict,
and never a test to run on someone else's writing.
The source page adds a warning that is easy to over-read, so read it
precisely. It says do not treat these signs as the defects to be fixed,
because sanding them off 'could just make detection harder' WITHOUT
MAKING THE WRITING BETTER. That is written for curators triaging
submissions to a shared encyclopedia, where the harm is a reviewer being
evaded. It is not an argument against drafting with a model, and it is
not an argument against a rewriter existing.
The part that generalises is the second clause. A tell list is a symptom
list, and prose optimised to minimise it is bland rather than human —
which is why nothing downstream may use this catalog as a target. Give a
reviser the author's voice and corpus as its objective; give it this
catalog as one diagnostic among several.

wp-signs.title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
wp-signs.note: Canonical community-maintained list; least commercially motivated source available. Fetched and extracted directly for this catalog.

wp-talk.title: Wikipedia talk:Signs of AI writing (+ Archive 1, Archive 2)
wp-talk.note: Retrieved with both archives. This is what the `confidence` field is built on: it records which patterns editors treat as strong and which they argue about. It is also where `transition-overload` is recorded as tested and demoted — see the `rejected` block. Not read: Archive 3+, whose existence was not verified.

wp-cleanup.title: Wikipedia:WikiProject AI Cleanup
wp-cleanup.note: The remediation posture: verify before removing, check cited sources for legitimacy, preserve salvageable sources rather than deleting wholesale. Matters most for the revise pass in the prose-review bundle. Notably attaches no quantified confidence threshold to any of its tags.

recent.title: Secondary coverage of current-generation tells, 2025-2026
recent.note: Surveyed. Weight varies sharply and is recorded per entry. The strongest item is a 2026 arXiv study finding that purely STRUCTURAL narrative features separate AI from human fiction at 93.2% macro-F1 with no lexical features at all — which is the empirical case for this scanner's cadence half. The em-dash figures come from an independent 2026 measurement. Several widely repeated patterns trace to a single Forbes contributor piece with no dataset, and are labelled contested here. Much of the rest of this space is SEO marketing for detection and humanizer tools, with invented thresholds; none of it is used.

fixture.title: Observed in this repo's own regression fixture
fixture.note: script-v1-before.txt vs script-v2-after.txt — same author, same content, known answer.

local.title: Added during authoring, not yet corroborated by a primary source
local.note: Treat as provisional. Anything here should either earn a source or be dropped.

_about: Patterns deliberately NOT shipped, and why. Recorded rather than deleted
because a silently removed pattern gets re-added by the next person with
the same plausible idea. Everything here looked reasonable and lost.

announced-insight.was: Announcing an insight in place of delivering one ("here's the thing", "what most people miss").
announced-insight.why_rejected: Removed 2026-08-03 after shipping in v0.1. Three reasons, and the first alone is sufficient: it is NOT ON THE SOURCE PAGE. Verified against the full wikitext - the entry's own note conceded this, tracing it to a Forbes contributor piece with no counts and no control corpus, which is exactly the class of source this catalog labels contested and does not build on. Second, it duplicates not_deterministic.announced-then-undelivered, which declares the same phenomenon undecidable by regex; shipping a regex for it contradicted the catalog's own boundary. Third, CALIBRATION.md FP-2026-07-26-a logged it as the first field false positive and concluded it was 'an argument for pruning rather than tightening if it recurs'. It recurred. The standard already applied to false-range applies here.

transition-overload.was: Density of furthermore / moreover / additionally / it is worth noting.
transition-overload.why_rejected: Wikipedia's editors shipped this, tested it, and DEMOTED it to their Ineffective indicators section, on the reasoning that conjunction overuse 'is more of a byproduct of essaylike-writing that AI and humans engage in'. Their current page states only a few transition words are known to be overused. This catalog shipped it briefly in v0.1 and it immediately produced a false positive on this repo's own docs/wiring.md. Re-adding it repeats an experiment already run and already reverted.
transition-overload.replaced_by: didactic-disclaimer, which targets the narrower 'it is important to note' habit rather than conjunction density.

perfect-grammar.was: Flawless spelling and grammar as evidence of generation.
perfect-grammar.why_rejected: Listed as an ineffective indicator: many editors are skilled writers or come from professional writing backgrounds.

formal-register.was: Formal, academic, or elevated prose as evidence.
formal-register.why_rejected: Stated directly by the source: the correlation with AI 'does not extend to all formal, academic, or fancy-sounding prose'. This is also the failure mode that hits non-native English speakers hardest, and is the single most important thing this catalog must not do.

bland-or-robotic-prose.was: Prose that reads as flat or mechanical.
bland-or-robotic-prose.why_rejected: Listed as ineffective; usually reflects the reader's unfamiliarity with real AI patterns rather than a property of the text.

em-dash-density.was: Em dashes per 1000 words as a flagging signal.
em-dash-density.why_rejected: The numbers do not support it. A 2026 measurement REPORTEDLY puts the human baseline at mean 3.23 per 1000 words with a range of 0.33 to 17.12 — a fiftyfold spread — while current models have moved BELOW that mean (GPT-5.4 at 1.43, Gemini 2.5 Flash at 1.28). Only the aging 4.x generation sits clearly above it. CAVEAT, and it matters because these figures are the whole argument for this rejection: they come from `sources.recent`, the one source entry with no URL, so they are secondhand and currently uncitable — see the callout in the bundle README. The rejection does NOT rest on them alone. Wikipedia's talk page is independently its most-argued item, with editors calling it weak and noting the essay itself is full of them; and this repo's own docs measure 11-18 per 1000 first-hand, which a gate keyed on em dashes would flag. Em-dash rate is still MEASURED and REPORTED here, because it is useful context about a document's texture, but it never flags.

curly-quotes.was: Typographic quotes and apostrophes as evidence.
curly-quotes.why_rejected: Word processors have auto-formatted these for over a decade, and Gemini and Claude typically do not emit them at all. Measured and reported, never flagged.

synonym-expansion.was: Expanding flagged vocabulary into synonym sets.
synonym-expansion.why_rejected: The source is explicit: 'This section is to be taken as literally as possible: a word being overused by AI does not imply that its synonyms are also overused.' Entries here match the attested word, not its neighbourhood.

additionally-initial.why_rejected: TESTED AND REJECTED 2026-08-04 on corpus evidence. This was proposed to correct what looked like an over-generalisation in the `transition-overload` rejection: that entry was dropped for transition DENSITY, while the source page separately lists 'Additionally (especially beginning a sentence)' as its first AI-vocabulary item, with two citations. So a narrow sentence-initial form seemed defensible. It is not. Measured on the acceptance corpus it appears in 1 of 33 AI documents and 1 of 12 provably-human ones — proportionally MORE common in human writing. The original rejection was right for a reason its author did not have: not merely that density is the wrong statistic, but that the word does not discriminate at all in encyclopedic register. Recorded so the same reasonable-looking case is not re-argued a third time.

copulative-avoidance.was: Replacing 'is/are' with functions as, operates as, refers to, holds the distinction of being.
copulative-avoidance.why_rejected: TESTED AND REJECTED 2026-08-04. The source page devotes a section to this and it is plainly real as an observation about register. The deterministic form is not usable: measured on the acceptance corpus, the broad version appears in 4 of 33 AI documents (12%) and 1 of 12 human ones (8%) — encyclopedic prose says 'functions as a' constantly and means it. Narrowing to the distinctive constructions ('holds the distinction of being', 'ventured into') dropped it to 0 of 33 AI documents: precise enough to be useless. The pattern lives between two failure modes with no gap between them. `serves-as` and `boasts` already cover the two variants that do discriminate. What remains needs a parser that can tell a copula-avoidance from a verb doing real work, which is out of scope here and belongs with the critics.
copulative-avoidance.measured: broad: 4/33 AI, 1/12 human (raw matches). narrow: 0/33 AI.

_about: Patterns the brief asks for that a regex genuinely cannot decide. Recorded
here so the gap is documented rather than quietly dropped, and so the
Phase 2 critics know what they own exclusively. Do not add regexes for
these — an approximation would fire on everything and teach people to
ignore the whole tool.
not_deterministic.llm-safe-truths: Unfalsifiable filler sentences that pad without adding information. Detecting them requires knowing what the sentence claims and whether the claim could be wrong.
not_deterministic.announced-then-undelivered: An insight announced and never actually delivered. Needs the surrounding argument.
not_deterministic.surveying-without-committing: Presenting positions without defending one. A whole-document property.
not_deterministic.absence-of-concrete-detail: No name, number, date, place, or quoted phrase where one belongs. Absence is not matchable. ADJUDICATED BY NOBODY: prose-pattern-critic shipped owning this and was measured out of it - worst true-positive rate of its five patterns and its largest source of false positives on published human prose, at the same time. A stated gap, not an oversight; see that primitive's meta.yaml.
not_deterministic.no-voice-shift: Register that never moves with subject matter. Requires comparison across sections.
not_deterministic.invented-specifics: Concrete-sounding detail that is fabricated. Requires checking against the world.

entries.label: "commitment to excellence"
entries.note: Press-release phrasing; the source list flags it via quoted executive statements.

entries.label: comprehensive
entries.note: A checkable factual claim in technical writing, filler everywhere else. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: leverage (verb)
entries.note: Verb use with an object only, so financial and physical leverage are not matched. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: paradigm
entries.note: A term of art in programming and philosophy of science. Allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: robust
entries.note: Precise in statistics and systems engineering, filler in marketing. The clearest argument for per-register allowlists; allowlisted in `technical`.

entries.label: current-era participles (emphasizing / highlighting / showcasing)
entries.note: The mid-2025-onward cohort, and the reason this catalog is not just a list of words from 2023. Where the older tells were nouns (delve, tapestry), the surviving ones are participles. Bare use is ordinary English, so this is density-gated and weak; the high-severity signal is the same verbs in a significance-asserting tail clause, which `participle-tail` catches separately.

entries.label: enhance / align with
entries.note: Also mid-2025-onward. Ordinary in technical writing; watch the rate, not the presence.

entries.label: bustling
entries.note: Almost always promotional travel-brochure register.

entries.label: delve
entries.note: The signature tell of the 2023-24 generation. Largely trained out, so a hit now is notable.

entries.label: "dive into" / "deep dive"
entries.note: The replacement 'delve' was trained into. Same move, newer word.

entries.label: "ever-evolving landscape"
entries.note: Requires the modifier. Literal landscapes and 'the landscape of X' in geography are not matched.

entries.label: "foster a sense of"
entries.note: Requires the abstract object. Foster care and fostering animals are not matched.

entries.label: intricate
entries.note: Legitimate about genuinely intricate mechanisms; filler about ideas.

entries.label: "navigate the complexities"
entries.note: Deliberately requires an abstract object. Navigating a menu, a tree, or a ship is not a tell. Note the whole-word alternatives: lexical entries are wrapped in \b automatically, so a bare prefix like `complex` would fail to match `complexities`.

entries.label: tapestry (figurative)
entries.note: Figurative use only. Literal weaving is not matched.

entries.label: "in today's ... world" / "in an era of"
entries.note: The canonical throat-clearing opener.

entries.label: underscore (figurative)
entries.note: Verb form with an abstract object only. The typography character and identifier naming are not matched, and `technical` allowlists it anyway.

entries.label: actually
entries.note: Top hit in the session that motivated this primitive: eight occurrences the model's own self-assessment did not notice. Counting is what scripts are for.

entries.label: crucially / importantly / interestingly
entries.note: Sentence-adverb throat-clearing. Legitimate sparingly.

entries.label: genuinely
entries.note: Fine once. Six times in four thousand words is a tic, which is why this category is judged on density and never on presence.

entries.label: quiet / quietly
entries.note: Named in recent coverage as a current-generation adverbial tic.

entries.label: chat preamble leaked into the document
entries.note: The assistant's structural moves — offering, opening, signing off — left in a document. Distinct from `chatbot-register`, which catches its characteristic phrases. SHIPPED AS TIER A AND CORRECTED BEFORE RELEASE. Review found it firing on ordinary human correspondence: a business email closing 'Let me know if you need anything else before Friday' trips it, as does any customer-service reply. That is disqualifying for Tier A, whose contract is that no human writes the pattern in ANY register and whose acceptance gate asserts zero false positives on human text. The evidence for shipping it — 2 of 33 AI documents, 0 of 12 human — came from a corpus that is entirely encyclopedic prose, so it could not have exercised the register where the entry actually misfires. Clean on the corpus you have is not the same as clean. Now severity 3 style, density-gated, and disabled in `correspondence`. In article register it is still a strong signal; in email it is Tuesday. See CALIBRATION.md FP-2026-08-04-d.

entries.label: chatbot register leaked into the draft
entries.note: The assistant's conversational register, left in a document that is not a conversation. DEMOTED FROM TIER A on 2026-08-04, and the self-identification half promoted to its own Tier A entry (`model-self-identification`). The reason is a false positive that the acceptance corpus structurally could not surface. These phrases are ordinary business correspondence — 'I hope this helps', 'let me know if you need anything else' — and this bundle ships a `correspondence` profile as a first-class register. As Tier A they carried `always_flag` and bypassed density gating, so a single polite email sign-off tripped the tier whose entire claim is near-zero false positives. A corpus of 45 encyclopedic documents cannot exercise that. They remain a real signal IN ARTICLE REGISTER, which is why this is severity 3 rather than deleted, and why it is disabled in `correspondence` rather than everywhere. The general lesson is recorded in CALIBRATION.md FP-2026-08-04-d: a tell that is dispositive in one register and unremarkable in another is a STYLE entry, not an artifact, however obviously machine-like it looks.

entries.label: knowledge-cutoff or source-gap hedge
entries.note: A model describing its own epistemic position, or narrating the gaps in its retrieval. Neither belongs in a finished document.

entries.label: model markup artifact
entries.note: Literal strings no human types: citation scaffolding from ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and Perplexity that survived a copy-paste. These are ARTIFACTS, not style — dispositive rather than suggestive — so they bypass density gating entirely via always_flag. One occurrence is the finding. FIXED 2026-08-03: the separator was hardcoded to U+0007. That is how MediaWiki STORES these markers, not what a paste from the model contains - the real separator is a Private Use Area codepoint. So the entry matched the wiki RENDERING of the tell rather than the tell itself. It now accepts a PUA codepoint, BEL, or no separator at all, and covers the news/file/view turn types alongside search/image. Also adds attributableIndex, which the source page names in a section heading and this catalog had never matched, and the 'Brand+3Brand+3' citation pileup. Gaps here are the most expensive in the catalog: Tier A is the only dialect-neutral tier and the only thing --artifacts-only retains.

entries.label: the text says it is a language model
entries.note: Split out of `chatbot-register` on 2026-08-04, and the split is what makes Tier A's promise true rather than approximately true. TIER A MEANS NO HUMAN WRITES THIS IN ANY REGISTER. That is what earns `always_flag`, the bypass of density gating, and the acceptance gate's absolute zero-false-positives rule. Leaked markup qualifies. Unreplaced placeholders qualify. This qualifies: nobody describes themselves as a large language model. Chat pleasantries do not qualify, and that is why they are no longer here. 'I hope this helps' and 'let me know if you need anything else' are ordinary business email — they were sitting in the dispositive tier, in a bundle that ships a `correspondence` register as a first-class profile. Measured: they fire on unremarkable human correspondence, which means Tier A's absolute-zero claim was false for any author writing email. The acceptance corpus could not have caught it, being 45 documents of encyclopedic prose.

entries.label: unreplaced placeholder
entries.note: Template text the author never filled in. Trivially checkable and embarrassing to ship, which makes it worth catching even though it is rare.

entries.label: the challenges-and-future-prospects formula
entries.note: A whole-paragraph shape the source list names explicitly: 'Despite its [positive descriptor], [subject] faces challenges...' closing on speculation about future improvement. Distinctive because it is a template, not a phrase.

entries.label: compulsive summary
entries.note: HISTORICAL. The source files this under indicators from roughly 2023 and treats it as obsolete in newer models — formulaic conclusion sections restating the body. A hit today points at an older draft or a human writing habit more than at a current model.

entries.label: didactic disclaimer ("it's important to note")
entries.note: Replaces the `transition-overload` entry, which was REMOVED — see the `rejected` block. This narrower form is the disclaimer habit, not conjunction density. Historical: the source dates it Nov 2022-2024 and calls it obsolete in newer models, so a hit is more likely an older draft than a current one.

entries.label: enumeration scaffolding
entries.note: Announcing the shape of a list before giving it. 'Three reasons, and each one is worth sitting with.'

entries.label: false range ("from X to Y")
entries.note: A vague spectrum gestured at to imply comprehensiveness. TWO WARNINGS. (1) PROVENANCE: this is NOT in Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing — a targeted search of the raw wikitext found no such pattern. It was inherited from the design brief and is retained on this author's judgement alone, which is why severity is 2 and confidence is contested. (2) It over-fires: the prototype's version matched every date and number range ('From 1995 to 2003'). Numerals, currency, months, and weekdays are now excluded on both sides, and the construction must be sentence-initial or introduced by everything/ranging/spanning/covering.

entries.label: stacked hedging
entries.note: Two hedges doing one hedge's work.

entries.label: negative parallelism ("it's not X, it's Y")
entries.note: Widely treated as the strongest structural tell of the current generation, and reported at roughly 3x human rate - but that figure traces to a single news article with no published corpus study. Confidence is `medium` for that reason, and because the source page itself concedes the construction is 'common among human writers'. FALSE POSITIVES ARE DOCUMENTED AND SERIOUS: autistic writers and anyone with a formal rhetorical education report using deliberate parallel construction for decades, and binary contrast is a structural resource of English itself. THE RULE THAT SURVIVES SCRUTINY IS FREQUENCY AND PURPOSELESSNESS, NOT PRESENCE - one deliberate contrast is rhetoric; five paragraphs ending on the same shape is autopilot. Hence density-gating, like everything else. Pivot may be a comma, semicolon, or dash.  MEASURED COVERAGE, 2026-08-03: against the source page's own {{highlight}} examples quoted UNALTERED, this family covers 11 of 16, up from 4. Zero false positives across the repo corpus. Every one of the sixteen is asserted individually in selftest.mjs, gaps included, so the number cannot drift without a test failing.  Two things were wrong before that, and the second is the instructive one. (1) The pattern demanded a pronoun subject AND one of just/merely/simply/only, so the bare forms could not match. Subject is now any negated copula, the intensifier is optional, ain't/doesn't/don't/didn't are negators, and a second branch takes the bare 'not just X - they're Y' form that carries no copula at all. (2) THE FIRST FIX WAS VALIDATED AGAINST A FIXTURE THAT HAD BEEN RETYPED with ASCII apostrophes and spaced em dashes. The source page uses U+2019 and unspaced dashes. Scored against that laundered text the family looked like 7 of 9; scored against what the page actually says it was 1 of 9, because every contraction in this catalog was spelled with an ASCII apostrophe. Do not cite the 7/9 figure - it measured a fixture fitted to the code. The underlying defect was scanner-wide and is fixed at intake; see normaliseApostrophes().  THE CONTRACTED-RESUMPTION REQUIREMENT IS A FALSE-POSITIVE GUARD, NOT A CLAIM ABOUT ENGLISH. Relaxing the subject without it produced five hits on this repo's own prose, every one a legitimate explanatory contrast ('is not a decision, it is a migration'). Those five resume uncontracted; the source examples resume contracted. That is a split on a few dozen observations and nothing more. If it starts costing real detections, widen the pivot punctuation or prune the entry rather than adding epicycles.  Still missed, each for a stated reason: uncontracted verb resumption ('doesn't just undermine...; it questions'), which the guard above blocks; sentence-boundary contrast ('is not dissolution. Rather, it constitutes'); bare 'not X, but Y' with no copula; anaphoric repetition ('Not a career, not a body of work'), which needs its own entry and its own FP data; and 'X rather than Y', deliberately unshipped - it fires twice on this repo's clean-human fixture and the source marks it Grok-specific. See CALIBRATION.md FN-2026-08-03-a.

entries.label: "not just X, but Y"
entries.note: The compressed form of negative parallelism. Legitimate occasionally; a signature at volume.

entries.label: "not only ... but also"
entries.note: WIDENED 2026-08-03: `also` is now optional. The source page's Yayoi Kusama example reads 'not only a work of self-representation, but' with no `also`, so requiring it missed one of the page's own worked examples.  KNOWN EXPOSURE, and the measurement that found it is worth repeating because the first one was misleading. Widening was reported as '0 false positives across the repo corpus', which was true and nearly meaningless: this repo is technical register and technical register does not reach for this construction. Tested afterwards against ordinary formal prose, SIX OF SIX legitimate sentences match - 'She was not only the first to arrive but the last to leave', 'The treaty was not only unpopular but unenforceable'. The construction is ordinary English in essay and formal registers, and this entry cannot tell it from the AI-register version.  What holds the line is density gating, not the pattern: severity 2 with a min-count floor of 2, so a single occurrence never flags. An essayist who uses the construction habitually will still clear the ceiling, and for that author the honest fix is calibration - bands measured from their own corpus - rather than a narrower regex. Recorded here so nobody reads the repo-corpus zero as evidence it is safe everywhere.

entries.label: "is not X but Y"
entries.note: The source page gives this its own subsection under Negative parallelisms, and nothing in this catalog matched it before 2026-08-03: negative-parallelism required an intensifier and not-just-but requires one by construction, so the bare 'is not X but Y' form fell through the gap between them. The intensifier forms are deliberately excluded here by lookahead so the two entries cannot double-count the same sentence. Measured 0 false positives across this repo's 13 prose documents including both fixtures. Same caveat as its siblings: binary contrast is a structural resource of English, so this is density-gated and one occurrence means nothing. NOT SHIPPED alongside it: the source's third form, 'X rather than Y', which fires twice on script-v2-after.txt - this repo's canonical clean-human fixture - and which the source itself marks Grok-specific. That is the shape of a future CALIBRATION.md incident, so it stays out until there is a model axis to put it on.

entries.label: participle tail clause
entries.note: The tail that asserts significance instead of showing it. Restricted to significance-asserting verbs on purpose — generic tails (', allowing you to...') are ordinary English and would swamp this. WIDENED 2026-08-04 with the verbs the source page's own box lists and this pattern did not match: ensuring, encompassing, contributing, cultivating, fostering, enhancing, resonating, symbolising. The object list gains a/an/to/toward, since several of those verbs take them. Measured: +2 of 33 AI documents, +0 of 12 human, +0 on this repo.

entries.label: "overall," / "in short,"
entries.note: Milder than the explicit summary markers and often legitimate. Separated so the strong form is not diluted by the weak one.

entries.label: rule of three (X, Y, and Z)
entries.note: The rule of three: three-item lists, and adjective-adjective-adjective. Named on the source page. Contested and severity 1 because it matches ordinary English - any three comma-separated words - so it is meaningful only at density and never on presence.  RESTORED 2026-08-04, having been deleted earlier the same day. The deletion was wrong and the way it was wrong is worth more than the entry.  It was removed on measurements from a corpus that was silently corrupt: the human samples carried pre-ChatGPT revision metadata above text fetched from the CURRENT article, because prop=extracts accepts a historical revision id and serves the live page anyway. Against that phantom corpus the entry looked like an anti-signal - 84% of AI documents, 92% of human ones - and a standing rule in CALIBRATION.md said to delete on a field false positive.  Re-measured against the corrected corpus it is a weak POSITIVE signal: it flags on 36% of AI documents against 17% of human ones, roughly two to one. Holding the profile constant, deleting it halved recall at `technical` (6% to 3%) for no precision gain at all, and at `essay` traded 9 points of recall for 8 of precision. Either way the deletion was not a good trade for a tool whose output is explicitly leads rather than verdicts. A NUMBER RETRACTED HERE: an earlier draft of this note said the deletion cost 'seven times' the recall, comparing 21% to 3%. Those are `essay`-with against `technical`-without. The profiles carry different thresholds, so that figure measured the profile and not the entry. It is the same cross-setup error as the corrupt corpus that caused the deletion, made while correcting it.  The rule that survives: a field false positive is grounds to EXAMINE an entry, not to delete it. Deletion needs the cost measured too. See CALIBRATION.md FN-2026-08-04-b.

entries.label: "whether you're X or Y"
entries.note: Direct-address audience enumeration; marketing-copy scaffolding.

entries.label: "boasts a"
entries.note: Press-release verb. A building does not boast.

entries.label: "nestled in" / "in the heart of"
entries.note: Travel-brochure register, and one of the most distinctive single tells on the source list.

entries.label: canned assertion of notability and coverage
entries.note: Asserting that a subject is notable, and that sources exist, instead of demonstrating either. The source page singles this out as MORE COMMON IN TOOLS RELEASED IN 2025 OR LATER, which makes it one of the few entries here aimed at the current cohort rather than a trained-out one; the rest of the `current-era` material is two weak lexical entries. MEASURED on the acceptance corpus: 2 of 33 AI documents, 0 of 12 provably-human ones, 0 across this repo's prose. Weak but clean. Severity 2 and density-gated, so it needs a second occurrence to flag. WHERE THIS WILL MISFIRE: writing ABOUT notability — a Wikipedia policy discussion, a media-studies paper, a press kit. Those legitimately discuss independent coverage and trade publications. Mention-vs-use again, and unfixable for the same reason.

entries.label: "reflects a broader" / "part of a broader"
entries.note: Zooming out to significance the piece has not earned.

entries.label: "stands as" / "serves as"
entries.note: Narrowed to the significance-asserting objects. 'Serves as the entry point' is ordinary technical prose and is not matched.

entries.label: significance assertion
entries.note: Asserting that something mattered instead of showing that it did.

entries.label: vague attribution
entries.note: High confidence because it is checkable: either the citation is there or it is not. The prose-substance-critic in the prose-review bundle inherits every hit. WIDENED 2026-08-04 with forms from the source's box that the original missed, notably the noun-interposed 'some critics argue' — the old alternation required the verb to follow 'some' directly. Measured: +1 of 33 AI documents, +0 human, +0 on this repo. BOUNDARY REGRESSION, found and fixed 2026-08-04 before release: the widening spliced new alternatives onto the end of the pattern and dropped the trailing word boundary that closed the original alternation. Trigger words then matched as prefixes - 'Many scholarship programs' matched via 'many scholars', 'scientists believed' via 'scientists believe'. The 45-document corpus did not contain such a case, so nothing failed. A paired negative test now covers it. Splicing onto a regex tail is how a boundary gets lost silently; wrap the group instead.

entries.label: vibrant / rich / compelling
entries.note: Ordinary adjectives that cluster in generated prose. Weak alone, informative as a rate.
